commentary.meaning: Four separate meditation verses stand between the ritual preparation and the first of the thousand names, and they are not one picture but four. The first sets her before the eye as a woman the colour of vermilion, three-eyed, a ruby crown flashing above her and the lord of stars — the moon — in her hair, a jewelled goblet in one hand and a red lotus in the other, her reddened feet resting on a jewelled vessel; a gentle form, and the only one of the four that puts no weapon in her hands. The second exchanges cup and lotus for the noose, the goad, the flower-arrow and the bow, rings her about with the eight powers beginning with aṇimā as though they were rays thrown off her own body, and then closes the distance between the one meditating and the one meditated upon: I contemplate Bhavānī as nothing other than "I". The third seats her on a lotus, gold in colour and robed in yellow, a golden lotus shining in her hand, and calls her outright Śrīvidyā — the mantra herself wearing a body. The fourth is the shortest and the most concrete: this is the form to hold at the moment of counting the mantra, saffron-smeared, musk on the forehead, faintly smiling, red from garland to garment, bright as the hibiscus flower. Read in order the four move outward from an image held at arm's length, through an identity assumed, and back down into the plain act of sitting and reciting.
commentary.history:
These verses are not part of the thousand names and were not composed by whoever composed the stotra. They belong to the ritual apparatus that grew up around it, and the recension this site follows preserves that apparatus intact. Before the dhyāna comes the nyāsa, which declares the credentials of what is about to be recited: the seers of this great mantra are the Vāgdevatās headed by Vaśinī, the metre is anuṣṭubh, the deity is Śrī Lalitā Parameśvarī. Then the syllables aiṃ, klīṃ and sauḥ are placed on the fingers and on six points of the body. Then these four dhyāna verses. Then a five-fold offering in which each element of the world is given to her by its seed-syllable — laṃ for earth as scent, haṃ for space as flower, yaṃ for air as incense, raṃ for fire as lamp, vaṃ for the nectar-principle as food. Only after all of that does the manuscript say, plainly: "and then let him do the recitation." The dhyāna is the hinge. Everything before it prepares a body; everything after it is speech.

The three seed-syllables of that nyāsa are worth pausing over, because they are the three segments of the fifteen-syllabled mantra of this tradition. The nyāsa names them as such: the vāgbhava segment is called the bīja, the middle segment the śakti, the third segment the kīlaka or pin. So the reciter is being told, in code, that the sahasranāma is an unfolding of the pañcadaśākṣarī — that the thousand names are that mantra written out at length. This is the single most important background fact about the text, and it is stated before the first name is spoken.

The four verses themselves come from different places and do not agree with one another. Editions differ over how many to print and in what order; some manuals give one, some three, some five. The first, in the long śārdūlavikrīḍita metre, is close to the standard visualisation of Tripurasundarī found in tantric worship manuals, where she is soft, seated, and holds a cup rather than a weapon. The second is by far the most quoted, and is often chanted alone. The third is the only one that names her as Śrīvidyā outright. The fourth announces its own occasion in its last words: japa-vidhau smarāmi, "at the time of japa I call to mind."

Three of the four insist on red. Sindūra, aruṇa, the japā blossom, kuṅkuma, an aruṇa garland, aruṇa ornaments, aruṇa cloth. This is not decoration. In Śrīvidyā red is the colour of icchā, of desire understood as the first stirring by which anything at all comes to be, and of rajas taken as creative urgency rather than as agitation. The stotra's own third verse will make the point at cosmic scale: her red radiance rises like a flood until the world-eggs float submerged in it. Set this against Sarasvatī's white and Kālī's black and you have located this goddess precisely.

The last thing the dhyāna does is the most radical. Having built an image with great care, the second verse dissolves the arrangement in three words: aham ity eva vibhāvaye — I contemplate her as simply "I". The verb vibhāvaye is not "I worship" or "I see"; it is "I bring into being by imagining". The tradition is telling you, before the stotra begins, that the thousand names are not a description of somebody else. Every name you are about to say is in the third person and none of them is.
commentary.practice:
Each of the four verses is in a different metre, and knowing which one you are in tells you where to breathe. The first is śārdūlavikrīḍita, nineteen syllables to the line with the break after the twelfth: sindūrāruṇavigrahāṃ trinayanāṃ | māṇikyamaulisphurat. The second alternates eleven-syllable and twelve-syllable lines in the aupacchandasika pattern, which is why it feels lighter and quicker than the others. The third is sragdharā, twenty-one syllables in three even groups of seven: dhyāyet padmāsanasthāṃ | vikasitavadanāṃ | padmapatrāyatākṣīṃ. The fourth is pṛthvī, seventeen syllables with the pause after the eighth — which in this verse falls inside a word, sakuṅkumavilepa|nāmalikacumbikastūrikāṃ, so hear the pause without opening a gap in the sound.

The single most useful drill in the whole set is in the first line. Sindūrāruṇa has a retroflex ṇ: the tongue-tip curls back and strikes the hard palate. Trinayanāṃ, immediately after, has three dental n sounds: the tongue-tip goes forward to the back of the upper teeth. The two are only a few syllables apart and most English speakers flatten both into one sound. Run the line slowly until you can hear the difference, and the rest of the stotra becomes much easier, because this contrast recurs on almost every page — karuṇā, caraṇa, aruṇa and bāṇa all take ṇ, while nāyaka, vadana and bhavānī keep n.

The three sibilants are the other trap, and the first verse gives you all of them within a few words: śekharāṃ has the palatal ś, vakṣoruhām has the retroflex ṣ inside the kṣ cluster, and saumyāṃ, smitamukhīm and sphurat have the plain dental s. Note also that sphurat is s plus an aspirated ph, not an English f; let the p and the breath be heard separately.

Grammatically these verses are one sentence each, and hearing that keeps you from stopping in the wrong place. The long chain of words ending in -āṃ and -īṃ are all accusatives, and they are all governed by a single verb that arrives late: dhyāyet in the first and third verses, vibhāvaye in the second, smarāmi in the fourth. Nothing is complete until that verb lands. Carry the whole chain of epithets forward on one arc of attention and release it only at parāmambikām, bhavānīm, sampatpradātrīm and ambikām respectively.

One small delight to listen for in the fourth verse: japākusuma, the hibiscus flower, and japavidhau, the rite of recitation. Long ā in the flower, short a in the rite. The poet has put the two side by side deliberately, so that the flower you are visualising and the act you are performing sound like the same word. Keep the vowel lengths clean and the pun stays audible.

In practice most reciters use one of these before beginning and not all four. If you are learning, the second verse is the one to memorise first: it is short, it names the four weapons that the stotra's next two verses will explain, and it ends with the line that tells you what kind of attention the whole recitation asks for.

001.subtitle: Born from the fire of awareness

commentary.meaning: The stotra opens with three names that begin in śrī- and two that say where she came from and why. The three place her, and they widen as they go: mother, then great empress, then mistress of the splendid lion-throne — from the most intimate word available in the language out to the most political, with the same honorific syllable struck at the head of each. Then the verse turns and tells her origin in two names. She was not born of a womb. She rose out of a sacrificial pit whose fire was consciousness itself, and she rose for a purpose that was not her own: the gods had an errand, and there was nothing else left to try. So before a single feature of her body is described, the text has established the two things it wants held together for the next thousand names — that she is at once the nearest thing and the highest, and that her appearing in the world was a response to a need rather than a display of power.
commentary.history:
The stotra sits inside a story, and the story is worth knowing because the first verse depends on it. In the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa there is a long section called the Lalitopākhyāna, the account of Lalitā, told by Hayagrīva — Viṣṇu in his horse-headed form, the patron of learning — to the sage Agastya. The pūrvapīṭhikā preserved with this text opens with Agastya's complaint. You have told me everything, he says: her manifestation, her coronation, the killing of Bhaṇḍāsura, the description of Śrīpura, the greatness of the fifteen-syllabled mantra, the six placements, the inner and the outer worship, the rules of japa and of the fire offering, the secret identity of the Śrīcakra with the mantra and with the goddess herself. You have even given me the thousand names of Mantriṇī and of Daṇḍinī, her two commanders. You have not given me hers. Was it forgetfulness, or did you look past it on purpose? Hayagrīva answers that he withheld it because it is rahasya, a secret, and that he will give it now because Agastya has asked a second time and asked in devotion.

The text then makes an unusual claim about its own authorship. It says the stotra was not written by any human seer. Lalitā summoned the goddesses of speech — the Vāgdevatās headed by Vaśinī — and commanded them: you who know the secret of my cakra, who are devoted to my names, whom I have appointed to bestow eloquence on my devotees, compose a hymn marked with my thousand names, so that when my devotees praise me with it I am pleased at once. The Vāgdevatās did as they were told and later recited it before her in full assembly. This is why the nyāsa that precedes the recitation names them, and not a human ṛṣi, as the seers of the mantra. Eight of them are worshipped in the eighth enclosure of the Śrīcakra, and the stotra will name them later in its own course.

The repeated śrī- of the first three names is not filler required by the metre. Śrī means light, beauty, prosperity, and it is also the name of Lakṣmī; but in this tradition it is above all the badge of the school itself — śrīvidyā, śrīcakra, śrīpura, śrīguru, śrīmātā. Beginning three names in a row with it announces the lineage in the first breath. It is also an auspicious opening in the ordinary literary sense: a Sanskrit work is expected to begin with a word of good omen, and this one begins with three.

Cidagnikuṇḍasambhūtā is the name that carries the mythology. Bhaṇḍāsura had made the three worlds intolerable, and the gods, having exhausted every other course, performed a great sacrifice. In the fullest tellings the offering they finally made was themselves: they entered the fire. Out of that fire she rose. The name insists that the fire was not the ordinary sort. Cit is consciousness; the kuṇḍa is the pit dug for the sacred fire; she is what came up out of a fire-pit made of awareness. The Devī Māhātmya had told a structurally identical story some centuries earlier, in which the gods' massed brilliance condenses into a woman who fills the three worlds — but there the material is tejas, radiance, and here it is consciousness itself, which is a sharper and more philosophical claim.

Devakāryasamudyatā completes the thought. Samudyatā is a participle built on sam + ud + √yam, literally "risen up and braced for", the word you would use of somebody who has stood up and is already moving toward the task. She did not appear and then decide what to do. She came up out of the fire already committed. As for the errand itself, Bhaṇḍāsura will occupy the stotra again around its eightieth name, and by name 82 the text will say flatly that his city of Śūnyaka was burnt to nothing along with him by the Kāmeśvara weapon. What is worth noticing here is where he came from. When Śiva burnt Kāma to ash with the fire of his third eye, someone gathered the ash and shaped a figure from it — Citrakarman, one of Śiva's attendants, in the most common telling, though the accounts vary and some name a different gaṇa. Śiva's glance brought the figure to life and granted it the boon that any enemy who faced it would forfeit half his strength. An exclamation of astonishment — bhaṇḍa! — gave it its name, attributed to Brahmā in some recensions and to the assembled attendants in others. The demon that the goddess of desire was raised to destroy was himself made out of the ashes of desire.

The lion-throne of the third name is not a metaphor either. In the Lalitopākhyāna her enthronement is a distinct event, the paṭṭābhiṣeka that Agastya lists among the things he has already been taught, and the frame narrative uses the same epithet of her without explanation: siṃhāsaneśvarī always shows favour to the one who worships her. The verse is putting a coronation and a birth into the same four lines, in that order — sovereignty first, and only then the account of how she came to be.
commentary.practice:
This is an anuṣṭubh, the ordinary thirty-two syllable verse of Sanskrit narrative and hymn, and the nyāsa that precedes the stotra names anuṣṭubh as its metre. Four groups of eight; the natural breath is after the sixteenth syllable, at the end of siṃhāsaneśvarī. Within that, the first verse of the stotra is built on a small crescendo that is worth hearing. Śrīmātā is three syllables, śrīmahārājñī is five, and together they exactly fill the first quarter. Śrīmatsiṃhāsaneśvarī is eight and fills the second by itself. Then each half of the second line is a single eight-syllable name. Three names, then two, and each one longer than the last until they cannot grow any further.

The hardest sound here is ज्ञ in mahārājñī. Reciters trained in the north will say something close to "gy" and reciters trained in the south something close to "jñ"; the value the grammarians describe is j followed by the palatal nasal ñ, both made at the same place as the y in "yes". Say rāj-ñī with the tongue-body flat against the hard palate for both consonants. You will hear the other pronunciation on most recordings and there is nothing wrong with it, but this is what the letter is.

Three other points of care. In śrīmat-siṃhāsaneśvarī, a dental t runs straight into a dental s; release the t audibly rather than letting it collapse into the sibilant. In cidagni, the d is the giveaway of a sandhi: the word is cit, consciousness, and its final unvoiced t has been voiced by the vowel that follows, so what you are actually saying is cit + agni. Knowing that keeps the meaning of the name in view while you chant it. And kuṇḍa gives you the retroflex pair ṇḍ — tongue-tip curled back for both consonants, no forward movement between them.

The long vowels carry the line: śrī, -mātā, -rājñī, -eśvarī, -bhūtā, -dyatā. Every one of the five names ends in a long ā, because every one is a feminine nominative singular agreeing with an unspoken "she is". That is the grammatical shape of nearly the entire stotra: a thousand adjectives in search of a subject who never needs to be named.

For the recitation done as archanā rather than as stotra, each name is turned into the dative and given an offering — śrī mātre namaḥ, śrī mahārājñyai namaḥ, and so on down the list. It is worth practising the first verse both ways once, because hearing śrīmātā become śrī mātre teaches more about the fourth case than a paradigm chart will.

As for what to hold in mind: the order of the five names is itself the instruction. She is mother before she is empress, and she is on the throne before you are told where she came from. If the verse is to be used as a contemplation on its own — and it often is, being complete in itself — the thing to rest on is the fourth name. Everything that follows in the next thousand names comes out of a fire that is made of nothing but awareness.

002.subtitle: Four arms, and the noose of desire

commentary.meaning: Having said where she came from, the stotra now looks at her, and the first thing it reports is light: not the sun at noon but a thousand suns caught in the act of rising. The participle udyat holds them at the horizon, still climbing. Then the plain fact of four arms, and then the first two of the four things those arms hold. What is remarkable is that the verse refuses to leave the weapons as weapons. The noose, it says, is made of rāga — the pull of attachment, the wanting that draws a creature toward whatever it loves. The goad is anger, given the shape of an elephant-hook. These are not implements for use against an enemy standing somewhere outside her. They are the two forces that move every living thing, held in her own hands as her own equipment, and the half-verse sets up the pattern that the next verse will complete: four arms, four objects, and every object an aspect of mind.
commentary.history:
The four things in her hands are Kāmadeva's. The god of desire carries a bow and flower-arrows in Sanskrit poetry from a very early date, and the noose and the elephant-goad belong to the older Śākta armoury; this goddess holds all four. That combination is the visual signature of Tripurasundarī, and it is also the plot of the story the stotra is embedded in. Kāma was burnt to ash by Śiva; from that ash Bhaṇḍāsura was made; she rose from the fire to destroy Bhaṇḍāsura, and in the Lalitopākhyāna she afterwards restores Kāma to life at Rati's plea. Between the burning and the restoring, the weapons are in her hands. The iconography is the narrative frozen at its midpoint.

The standard reading in the tradition assigns the four objects to the three powers by which the divine is said to act: the noose is icchā, will or desire; the goad is jñāna, knowledge; and the bow with its arrows together are kriyā, action. On that reading the pair named in this verse are the two that come first — she wants, and she knows, and only then does she act. It is a scheme rather than an exegesis, and different teachers push it in different directions, but it is old and it is worth knowing because it explains why the noose is always named before the goad.

The more interesting move in this verse is grammatical. Rāga-svarūpa and krodha-ākāra are not the same kind of statement. Svarūpa is own-form, essential nature: the noose does not represent desire, it is desire. Ākāra is shape or configuration: the goad has the outline of anger. The tradition generally reads the noose as what binds a creature and the goad as what pulls it back, and the difference between the two words fits that. Attachment is what you are made of; anger is a shape imposed from outside, a hook in the flank that turns the animal around. Both are in her hands. Neither is renounced.

That refusal to renounce is the distinguishing mark of this stream of practice. A great deal of Indian religion treats rāga and dveṣa, attraction and aversion, as the two afflictions to be uprooted; the Yoga Sūtra lists them among the kleśas. Here the same two are the goddess's own regalia. Śrīvidyā does not deny that desire binds — the noose is a noose — but it insists that the binding force and the liberating force are one power differently directed, and that the rope is being held at the other end by someone who loves you. Bhāskararāya and the commentators after him spend a good deal of ink on exactly this point.

As for the thousand rising suns: the image is conventional, but the choice of the present participle is not. A risen sun is a fact; a rising sun is an event. She is described in the tense of something perpetually beginning, which matches the aruṇa, dawn-coloured, reddish theme that runs through the dhyāna verses and will return in the next verse as a flood of red light drowning the worlds. Some later reciters connect the thousand suns with the thousand names themselves, one for each ray. That is a pleasant idea and probably a late one; the text does not say it.
commentary.practice:
The verse contains three of the most awkward consonant clusters in the first ten śloka, and they are all worth slowing down for. Udyad-bhānu has d + y and then a d running into an aspirated bh; keep the aspiration on the bh and do not let it become a b. Pāśāḍhyā has ḍh, the voiced retroflex aspirate, which is one of the rarest and hardest sounds in the language: tongue-tip curled back, voice on, and a distinct puff of breath released as it comes away. And ujjvalā is j + j + v — a doubled palatal followed by a semivowel, and the place where most learners simply give up and say "ujwala". Take it as uj-jva-lā and hold the doubled j long enough to hear it as two.

The two long compound names in the second line are built to be heard as a pair, and the pairing is exact: rāga-svarūpa-pāśa-āḍhyā against krodha-ākāra-aṅkuśa-ujjvalā. Emotion, then the word for form, then the weapon, then a word meaning "rich in" or "blazing with". If you feel the parallel while chanting, the second line stops being a mouthful and becomes a sentence with a shape. Note too that the two words for form are deliberately different — svarūpa and ākāra — and the difference is audible. Do not let them blur.

Vowel length does most of the work of the metre here. Hold the ā in sahasrā-bhā, in cātur-bāhu (the ā of catur is short, the ā of bāhu is long — a common slip), in -āḍhyā, and in -ākāra-. The short a of krodha and of the final -kuśa- must stay short or the line will sag.

One sandhi to see in the written form. Krodha + ākāra gives krodhākāra, and ākāra + aṅkuśa gives ākārāṅkuśa: two long ā vowels swallowing each other twice in the same word. In the Devanagari it shows as a single ा each time, so the eye has to reconstruct what the ear cannot hear. This is the commonest reason a learner mis-parses a long name in this stotra, and it is worth pausing on the word क्रोधाकाराङ्कुशोज्ज्वला until the four pieces separate cleanly.

What to hold while chanting: the verse is asking you to identify what is pulling you and what is turning you back, and then to notice that both cords run to the same hand. The traditional counsel here is not to fight the noose. Watch where it is attached.

003.subtitle: The sugarcane bow and the five arrows

commentary.meaning: The other two hands, and then a change of scale. The bow she draws is made of sugarcane, and sugarcane, the name says outright, is the mind: sweet, jointed, and springing back when it is bent. The arrows are the five tanmātras, the bare qualities of sound, touch, form, taste and smell out of which everything sensed is constructed. Set this beside the previous verse and the inventory is complete, and it turns out to be an account of how experience happens at all: the mind is the bow that gives the shot its force, the five sense-qualities are the shafts, desire is the cord that draws, anger is the hook that turns you back. Then the third name abandons the whole apparatus. The rosy light of her own body rises like a tide until the entire ring of world-eggs floats submerged in it. The weapons were small and held in hands; this last name has no edge at all, and the universe is inside it.
commentary.history:
Kāmadeva's five arrows are traditionally flowers, and the list usually given names them: lotus, aśoka, mango-blossom, fresh jasmine and blue water-lily. Here they are not flowers. They are the five tanmātras — śabda, sparśa, rūpa, rasa and gandha, sound, touch, form, taste and smell — which is a term borrowed straight out of Sāṃkhya. In that system the tanmātras are the subtle, uncompounded precursors from which the five gross elements are produced; they stand between the sense of individuality and the material world. Making them her arrows is therefore a much larger claim than making them the five occasions of desire. Her shafts are not what tempts you; they are what the world you are tempted by is built out of.

This kind of substitution is characteristic. Śrīvidyā inherited an iconography from erotic poetry and a vocabulary from classical philosophy, and it reads the one through the other with complete confidence. The sugarcane bow gets the same treatment. Sugarcane is Kāma's bow because it is sweet; it becomes the mind because the mind is what has to be bent before an arrow can go anywhere. The Kaṭha Upaniṣad had used a different vehicle for the same anatomy — a chariot, with the senses as horses and the mind as the reins — and the parallel is close enough that the substitution here reads as deliberate rather than merely clever.

The third name changes register completely, and it is the longest word so far: sixteen syllables, filling the entire second line by itself. Nija means her own, not derived or borrowed; aruṇa-prabhā is the reddish light of dawn; pūra is a flood or a rising tide; majjat is a present participle, drowning or being submerged, still happening; brahmāṇḍa-maṇḍala is the whole circle of world-eggs. The name is one long image with the verb in the middle of it, and the tense matters: the worlds are not going to be flooded and were not flooded once, they are being flooded now.

Brahmāṇḍa is also, of course, the name of the purāṇa this stotra comes from. The Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa is one of the eighteen great purāṇas, and it is the text within which the whole Lalitā material — the narrative, this hymn, the ritual instructions — is transmitted; the Adhyātma Rāmāyaṇa is traditionally attached to it as well. The coincidence of the word is worth registering. The book is named for the cosmic egg, and here the egg is described floating in her light like something dropped into water.

One further point about the red. It has now appeared in every verse: sindūra and aruṇa in the meditation verses, a thousand rising suns in the last one, and now a flood of it. In Śrīvidyā this colour belongs to kāmakalā, the point at which pure consciousness first inclines toward manifestation, and it is the reason the goddess of this tradition is red where Sarasvatī is white. A verse that has just finished describing the mind as a bow and the senses as arrows ends by saying that the light in which all of this is happening is her own body — which is the whole argument of the tradition in a single compound.
commentary.practice:
Two sandhis are hidden in this verse and both are visible in the Devanagari once you know to look. Manorūpa plus ikṣu gives manorūpekṣu: a final a and an initial i have fused into a single e, written with the small stroke े over रू and प. Nija plus aruṇa gives nijāruṇa, two a sounds merged into one long ā. Neither juncture can be heard, so the reader has to reconstruct it from the sense. Practising these two words slowly — मनोरूपेक्षु and निजारुण — teaches more about vowel sandhi than a table of rules, because here you can see exactly what has gone missing.

The clusters to isolate: kṣu in ikṣu, which is k followed by the retroflex ṣ and never an English "x"; ñca in pañca, where the ñ is a palatal nasal made at the same place as the c that follows it, so the tongue never has to move; and, hardest of all, majjad-brahmāṇḍa, where a doubled j runs into an unaspirated d and then straight into br. Break it as maj-jad-brah-māṇ-ḍa and rebuild it at speed.

The second half of the verse is a single sixteen-syllable name occupying both quarters, which means there is no natural pause after the eighth syllable. Reciters generally take a light breath after nijāruṇaprabhāpūra and then run the rest through. Doing that also happens to divide the compound at its correct joint, between the flood and the thing being flooded.

Retroflexes come thick here: the ṇ of -aruṇa-, the ṇḍ of brahmāṇḍa and the ṇḍ of maṇḍalā, all three in one line, with the ṭ-series never far away. Curl the tongue-tip back and leave it back through -māṇḍamaṇḍalā rather than resetting between the two ṇḍ pairs. In koḍaṇḍā, likewise, the ḍ and the ṇ are both retroflex and the two together should sound like a single gesture.

Watch the vowel lengths in the first name. Manorūpa has a long ū; ikṣu has a short i and a short u; kodaṇḍā has a long o and a long final ā. Learners tend to lengthen the u of ikṣu because of the long vowel in front of it, and the metre will tell you at once when you have.

For contemplation, this verse gives you an unusually concrete instruction. Take the four objects in order — mind, senses, desire, anger — and notice that in each case the thing that seems to be happening to you is being described as something she is holding. Then let the last name dissolve the arrangement: whatever is being aimed, and whatever is being hit, is inside the same red light.

004.subtitle: Flowering hair, a crown of rubies

commentary.meaning: Here the stotra begins the long description of her body that will run without a break from this verse down to her feet and end, thirty-nine names later, in the summary "adorned with every ornament". It starts at the top, and characteristically it starts not with the crown but with what is underneath it. Her hair shines, and it shines because four kinds of blossom are worked through it: campaka gold, aśoka orange-red, punnāga cream-white and the fragrant water-lily, four colours and four scents braided into one head of hair. Only then does the second name lift the eye to the diadem, tier upon tier of rubies — and even there the word the verse settles on is not the crown itself but its glittering. Both names are built the same way. A list of beautiful things is given, and then a past participle at the end says that something has been made lovely by them; and in each case the thing made lovely is her, which quietly reverses the usual direction of an ornament.
commentary.history:
This is the opening of what the poets call an aṅga-varṇana, a limb-by-limb description, running from the hair down to the feet. The second half of the Saundaryalaharī is organised the same way and in the same order, and reading the two side by side from here on is the single most useful thing a student of this stotra can do: they cover the same features, often with the same comparisons, and the differences show up sharply. In this stotra the sequence begins at name thirteen and ends at name fifty-one, after which she is seated on Śiva's lap and the poem turns from her body to her city and her powers.

The four flowers are specific plants and it is worth knowing them. Campaka is Michelia champaca, whose deep-yellow flowers have one of the strongest scents in the Indian garden. Aśoka is Saraca asoca, which puts out dense clusters of orange-red blossom close against the trunk; classical poetry holds that it flowers when a beautiful woman touches it with her foot, one of the standing conceits called dohada, the tree's longing. Punnāga is Calophyllum inophyllum, white-petalled with a yellow centre, heavily scented. Saugandhika is simply "the sweet-scented one" — Monier-Williams glosses the word itself as fragrant — and it is generally taken to be a white or blue water-lily. So the compound is not a vague heap of flowers. It is four named species, chosen so that the colours run gold, red, white and white and the fragrances layer.

The tradition does something characteristic with this image. It insists that the flowers are not lending her hair their fragrance but borrowing hers. Śaṅkara's verse on the same subject says outright that the blossoms of Indra's own garden take up residence in her hair in order to acquire the scent that is natural to it. The logic is the same as in the previous verses, where the weapons in her hands turned out to be made of the forces they represent: whatever is beautiful in the description is not being attributed to her, it is being derived from her.

Kuruvinda, the stone of the second name, is a genuinely ambiguous word, and it is a good illustration of why a single dictionary is not enough. Monier-Williams lists it as a kind of barley, as the fragrant grass Cyperus rotundus, as the tree Terminalia catappa, as a flower-bud, as black salt, as cinnabar — and, in the neuter, as a ruby. Ruby is the sense the commentators take here, and the context forces it: what else would be strung in rows on a diadem. Note that the first meditation verse has already crowned her with māṇikya, which is the ordinary word for a ruby. The same stone is being named twice with two different words, once in the ritual frame and once in the stotra, and the effect is cumulative rather than repetitive.

Red, again. Ruby, aśoka, and behind them the sindūra and aruṇa of the meditation verses and the flood of red light in the verse just past. By this point in the text a reader should stop treating the colour as ornament. It is the tradition's signature, and when the stotra later calls her sarvāruṇā, wholly crimson, at name forty-nine, it is only stating what the description has been saying all along.
commentary.practice:
For the first time the verse consists of exactly two names, each sixteen syllables long, each filling a complete line. Count them and you will find that campakāśokapunnāgasaugandhikalasatkacā and kuruvindamaṇiśreṇīkanatkoṭīramaṇḍitā are both precisely half an anuṣṭubh. From here on this becomes the normal shape of a verse in this stotra, and knowing it helps: when you begin a line you know you will not be allowed to stop until sixteen syllables have gone by.

Three pieces of word-formation are visible in the written text and worth pausing over. Campaka plus aśoka has become campakāśoka, two short a vowels fused into a single long ā and written with one ा — the reader has to supply the seam. Punnāga looks like a simple word but is not: the underlying form is puṃnāga, "elephant among men", and the nasal has assimilated to the n that follows and doubled it, which is why the Devanagari shows पुन्नाग with a conjunct. And saugandhika is su-gandha, "good scent", put through the vowel-strengthening called vṛddhi that turns an initial u into au — the same process that turns sundara into saundarya in the title of Śaṅkara's poem.

The verse also gives you two present participles in the compound-final form ending in -at: lasat, shining, and kanat, glittering. This ending is going to be everywhere in the stotra — udyat in verse two, majjat in verse three, vibhrājat in verse five, calat in verse six — so learn its shape now. Written लसत् and कनत्, with the virāma cancelling the inherent a, they are the stem of a present participle with nothing added.

For the consonants: keep aśoka's palatal ś distinct from saugandhika's dental s, and keep both distinct from the retroflex ṣ, which does not appear in this verse and whose absence is itself a useful thing to notice. Maṇi, śreṇī and maṇḍitā all take the retroflex ṇ; koṭīra takes the retroflex ṭ. In practice the second line is a retroflex exercise: let the tongue-tip stay curled back from -maṇi- through to -maṇḍitā and only come forward for the dentals.

On what to hold: the verse is the beginning of a very long act of looking, and the traditional counsel about such passages is not to rush them in order to reach the doctrine. There is no doctrine coming. The description is the point, and the four flowers are meant to be smelled one at a time.

005.subtitle: The eighth-night moon on her brow

commentary.meaning: Two names, and both of them are moons. The first says that her forehead — the broad, clear expanse of it — carries the same light as the moon on the eighth night of the waxing fortnight, which is the night the disc stands at exactly half and makes the shape of a brow. The second changes the scale: now the whole face is the moon, and the small dab of musk on it is doing what the dark blemish does on the real moon. The pairing is careful. The first name gives her a moon; the second makes her one, and then hands her the flaw as an ornament. Nobody has ever seen an unmarked moon, and the poet, instead of pretending otherwise, puts the mark on with a fingertip and turns it into cosmetics.
commentary.history:
The eighth lunar day is not chosen at random. On the aṣṭamī of the bright fortnight the moon shows exactly half its disc, so the figure is not the thin crescent that Śiva wears in his hair but a full broad arc — the shape of a forehead seen straight on. It is worth holding both moons in view. Śiva carries a fragment of the moon; here she does not wear one, she is the arc. The meditation verse had already called her tārānāyakaśekharā, crowned with the lord of the stars, so within a few lines the moon has been placed on her head, then identified with her brow, then with her whole face. The stotra is not repeating itself. It is tightening.

The second name contains a pun that is easy to walk past. Mṛganābhi, the word used here for musk, means literally "deer's navel", from the gland of the male musk deer from which the substance is taken. And one of the ordinary Sanskrit names of the moon is mṛgāṅka, "deer-marked", because the dark patches on the lunar surface were seen as a deer, just as they were seen elsewhere as a hare — hence the moon's other name, śaśāṅka. So the spot that the poet paints on her moon-face in order to imitate the moon's own spot is itself named after the animal that the moon's spot is traditionally taken to be. The image closes on itself. This is the kind of buried figure that Sanskrit poetics treats as the mark of a real poet, and it is a reason to take the Vāgdevatās' hymn seriously as literature and not only as liturgy.

Viśeṣaka is the technical word for a mark made on the forehead with sandal paste or a similar substance — the dictionary gives exactly that — so what is being described is a cosmetic tilaka of musk, not a natural mole. The detail is not new to the text. The fourth meditation verse, which comes from a completely different source, describes her as alikacumbikastūrikā, with musk kissing her forehead, using a different word for musk and a different word for forehead. Two independent formulations of the same observed image, sitting a few lines apart on the same page, is good evidence that both belong to a settled visual tradition rather than to one poet's invention.

One last word repays a look. Kalaṅka, the moon's spot, also means defamation, blame, a stain on a reputation. The commentators enjoy this. The only blemish anywhere near her is one that she has applied herself, deliberately, and that improves the face it is on.
commentary.practice:
Two more sixteen-syllable names, one per line, and both of them front-loaded with hard consonants. Aṣṭamī opens with ṣṭ, the retroflex sibilant running straight into the retroflex stop: the tongue-tip curls back for the ṣ and stays there for the ṭ, with no forward movement in between. This is the same cluster as in aṣṭa, eight, and in every word built on it, so it is worth twenty seconds of drilling.

The join between vibhrājat and alika shows the same sandhi you met in cidagni: a final unvoiced t before a vowel becomes a voiced d, giving vibhrājadalika, written विभ्राजदलिक. Seeing that lets you find the word-boundary the ear cannot hear, and it tells you that vibhrājat is another of this stotra's present participles in -at.

Sthala needs care. The th is an aspirated dental — t with a puff of breath — and never the English sound in "thing". Say s, then t, then release the breath: s-tʰa-la.

Mṛga contains a genuine syllabic vowel, ṛ. It is not the sequence "ri", though most northern reciters approximate it that way, nor "ru", though many southern reciters do. The grammarians describe a short r held as the nucleus of the syllable, made with the tongue in the retroflex position. Whichever regional habit you adopt, keep it short: mṛ is one beat, and lengthening it will throw the count of the line.

The ṅk of kalaṅka is the guttural nasal, made at exactly the place where the following k is made, so the tongue does not travel. And viśeṣakā gives you the palatal ś and the retroflex ṣ in adjacent syllables, vi-śe-ṣa-kā, which makes it one of the best two-second drills in the whole first ten verses. If you can hear the difference there, you can hear it anywhere.

As for what this verse asks of the attention: the two verses before it described power and the two after it will describe expression. This one describes a surface at rest. It is the still point of the opening sequence, and the traditional advice about the moon-images in this stotra is simply not to hurry them — a half-moon and a face are both things that reward being looked at longer than seems necessary.

006.subtitle: Love's archway and the darting fish

commentary.meaning: Both names in this verse turn her face into a place, and in both the place belongs to Kāma. In the first, her face is the house where Love's wedding is being held, and her two eyebrows are the festooned arch flung across its doorway — the toraṇa that is put up over the entrance for an auspicious occasion. In the second, the loveliness of that face brims over the way a full tank spills into its outlet channel, and her eyes move in the spill like fish in running water. Notice what the two names have in common: neither describes a feature, both describe a motion. An archway is a thing you pass under on the way in, and an overflow is water going somewhere. After the stillness of the previous verse, the face has begun to move.
commentary.history:
A toraṇa is not an architectural arch in general. It is the decorated gateway raised over a doorway for a festival or a wedding, hung with mango leaves, flowers and cloth; the word carries the occasion with it. So the first name is not saying that her brows are curved like an arch. It is saying that her face is a wedding house, that the wedding is Love's, and that the brows are the garland strung over the door to announce it. This is a forward reference. Twelve names later the stotra will describe the marriage thread that Kāmeśvara has tied around her neck, using the same word — māṅgalya — that appears here in māṅgalya-gṛha. The wedding announced at the eyebrows is celebrated at the throat.

The second name is one of the most quietly technical images in the whole hymn. Parivāha, in the dictionary, is the overflow of a tank and the channel dug to carry the surplus away: the word belongs to irrigation, not to poetry. The picture is therefore precise. Her face is a reservoir that has filled past its lip; the beauty running out of it has cut a channel; and in that channel there are fish. Śaṅkara uses the same rare word in the same position in the Saundaryalaharī, describing the parting of her hair as the outlet-channel of the flood of her facial beauty, which makes this one of the closest verbal contacts between the two texts.

The fish matter. In Sanskrit poetry a beautiful woman's eyes are conventionally compared to fish, and the comparison is not merely about shape: it is about the flicker, the fact that a fish in shallow water is visible chiefly as a movement. But the fish is also Kāma's emblem — he is makara-dhvaja and mīna-ketana, the god whose banner carries the sea-creature — so the second name, like the first, has quietly put Love's insignia on her face. Two names, two pieces of Kāma's wedding equipment: his archway and his flag.

One word here deserves an honest warning. Cillikā, the word for eyebrow, is not in Monier-Williams with that meaning. The 1899 dictionary records cilli as a bird of prey and cillī as a pot-herb, and cillikā only as a variant of those. The sense "eyebrow" is what the commentators take, it is what the context demands, and it is recorded in later Sanskrit lexicons and in the modern Indo-Aryan languages; but a student working only from Monier-Williams will not find it, and would be entitled to be puzzled. This is worth knowing as a general caution. The sahasranāma draws on a vocabulary that is partly regional, partly late, and partly technical to its own tradition, and the great colonial dictionary does not cover all of it.
commentary.practice:
Both lines are single sixteen-syllable names again, and both are long chains of nouns with a single word at the end that turns the chain into a description of her. Read the first as vadana - smara - māṅgalya - gṛha - toraṇa - cillikā: face, Love, auspicious, house, arch, eyebrow. The order is the order of the thought, from the largest container to the smallest thing described, and if you hold that shape the sixteen syllables come easily.

The consonant to watch in the first line is the ṅg of māṅgalya, a guttural nasal followed by a voiced velar, with the tongue-body making both at the same place. Then ly in māṅgalya and gṛ in gṛha, which contains another syllabic ṛ. Cillikā has a doubled l — cil-li-kā — and the doubling must be heard, because the metre counts the first syllable heavy on the strength of it.

The second line is harder. Vaktra opens with the cluster kt, unvoiced velar into unvoiced dental, and then r: vak-tra, three consonants with only one vowel among them. Lakṣmī has the kṣ conjunct followed immediately by m, so the word is really lakṣ-mī and the ṣ must be audible. Calanmīnābha hides a sandhi: the present participle calat, moving, has had its final t assimilated to the m that follows, giving calan-mīna — another instance of the -at participle, the fourth in six verses. And locanā ends the line with three light, open syllables, which is why the whole thing lands softly after so much consonantal traffic.

One rhythmic point. Both of these names describe motion, and the metre cooperates. The first line is dominated by long vowels — mā, gṛ is short but tora and cilli give a settled, arch-like shape — while the second accelerates through vaktra-lakṣmī and only opens out at parīvāha. Chanting them at the same speed flattens something the poet built in.

For contemplation, the tradition takes the eyebrows seriously for a reason beyond ornament. The point between the brows is where the ājñā-cakra is located, and Śaṅkara's poem places Śiva there. Whether or not you take that up as a practice, the verse gives you somewhere definite to rest the attention while chanting: the arch above the door, and then the water going past.

007.subtitle: A campaka bud, and a jewel that shames the stars

commentary.meaning: The whole verse is about the nose: one line for the nose itself and one for the ornament in it. The first calls it a daṇḍa, a stem or staff, and gives it the colour and slenderness of a campaka flower newly opened — the same pale gold that was braided into her hair four verses ago, now carried down onto the face, so that the poem's colour scheme holds. The second turns to the jewel worn in that nose, and the boast is precise: it does not merely outshine the stars, it puts them out of countenance. After the sweep of the eyebrows and the moving water of the eyes, the description has narrowed to about an inch of face, and it spends thirty-two syllables there. That deliberate slowing is part of what the head-to-foot form is for.
commentary.history:
Nāsādaṇḍa is a plant word. Daṇḍa is a stalk, a stem, a staff — the same word that gives the sugarcane bow of the third verse its shape — so the nose is being seen as something that grows straight up. Śaṅkara makes exactly the same move with a different plant, calling it nāsāvaṃśa, the bamboo of the nose, and adding a joke the sahasranāma does not risk: a bamboo is what a flag is flown from, so her nose is the flagstaff of the Himālaya's royal house. The two texts are working the same figure — straightness, slenderness, a segmented stem — from the same tradition of description.

Campaka has already been named in this stotra, in the fourth verse, among the flowers in her hair. Repeating it here is not carelessness. The campaka's yellow is a specific and rather pale gold, and using it twice ties the top of the head to the middle of the face. Nava, fresh or new, is doing work too: an opened campaka darkens as it ages, so the comparison is to the flower at its palest, on the first day.

The nose ornament is a South Indian detail. Temple images of the goddess in the far south are given a nose stud, often set with diamonds, and in living practice the ornament is one of the things a devotee may vow to give. Śaṅkara, describing the same feature, says she wears pearls, and offers an explanation of where they come from: her breath, being cool, condenses pearls inside the nostril, and the ornament outside is one of the surplus. That is a conceit rather than a doctrine, but it depends on the same observation the commentators build on — that this is the part of the face through which breath moves. Some read the two nostrils as the channels iḍā and piṅgalā, which is a commentarial overlay and not something the verse itself says.

One word here has more range than it looks. Tārā, in the compound tārākānti, is a star — the light this jewel defeats is starlight. But tārā is also the standard word for the pupil of the eye, and it is the name of one of the great goddesses of the tantric tradition. The plain sense in this verse is starlight; the other meanings sit close by, and a reader who has been through the meditation verses will already have met the moon there under the title tārānāyaka, lord of the stars. Something the moon rules over is here being outshone by a nose stud, which is the kind of quiet escalation the hymn goes in for.
commentary.practice:
Two words in this verse should be looked at together, because they are the same word twice: nāsādaṇḍa and nāsābharaṇa. The first begins with a dental n; the second begins with the same dental n and then ends in a retroflex ṇ. That final ṇ is not arbitrary. Ābharaṇa is built on the root bhṛ with the prefix ā, and the r inside the root pulls the following n back into the retroflex position — the rule the grammarians call ṇatva, which will account for the retroflex nasal in an enormous number of the names in this stotra. Once you have heard the difference between the n of nāsā and the ṇ of ābharaṇa inside a single word, that rule stops being abstract.

The compound-final ābha, appearing here in puṣpābha, is worth collecting. It means "having the look of" and it has now turned up four times in six verses: sahasrābhā in the second, kalaṅkābha in the fifth, mīnābha in the sixth, puṣpābha here. It is one of the handful of endings that do most of the work in this hymn, along with -maṇḍitā, -śobhitā, -virājitā and -bhāsurā, all of which mean roughly "made splendid by". Recognising them turns a long compound into a short one plus a familiar tail.

The two lines end with two different kinds of adjective and it is audible. Virājitā is a past participle: made brilliant, having been made resplendent. Bhāsurā is a primary adjective formed with the suffix -ura: simply shining, no agent implied. The first line therefore says something was done to her nose, and the second says her ornament shines of itself.

For the consonants: puṣpa has ṣ then p, retroflex sibilant into labial stop, and the ṣ must not soften into an s. Tirask-ārin gives you the rs sequence across a syllable boundary. And keep the long ā of nāsā long in both names — it is the same vowel twice in a row, and a common place to let the second one shorten.

On what to hold: this is the smallest thing the hymn has stopped for so far, and there will be smaller. The discipline the head-to-foot description asks for is the willingness to spend a whole verse on a nose without deciding that the poem must really be about something else.

008.subtitle: Kadamba flowers, and the sun and moon for earrings

commentary.meaning: The ears, and again a flower and a jewel, but this time the two are wildly out of scale with one another and the poet has set them side by side without comment. In the first name the ornament tucked over her ear is a sprig of kadamba blossom, the small orange globes that come out with the first rains, and the name ends by saying simply that she is heart-stealing because of it. In the second name the pair of pendants hanging from those same ears are the disc of the sun and the disc of the moon. A twig of flowers and the two lights of the sky, worn on the same head, in successive lines. Nothing in the verse reconciles them, and the refusal to reconcile them is the effect.
commentary.history:
The kadamba is her tree. Neolamarckia cadamba puts out dense spherical heads of orange flower at the beginning of the monsoon, and the association with this goddess is thoroughly established: Śaṅkara sets her island palace in a grove of them, using the synonym nīpa; this stotra will later call her kadambavanavāsinī, dweller in the kadamba grove, at name sixty, and kadambakusumapriyā, lover of kadamba blossoms, at name three hundred and twenty-three; and the great southern temple of Madurai remembers itself as having grown up in a kadamba forest. So the sprig over her ear is not a stray botanical detail. It is a badge, and by the time the reciter reaches name sixty the tree will have been named three times.

Karṇapūra, the word for the ornament, is itself half flower and half jewellery: the dictionary defines it as an ornament worn round the ear, especially one of flowers, and then goes on to list it as a name for the blue lotus and for the aśoka tree. That ambiguity is exactly what the name exploits. The tāṭaṅka of the second line is unambiguous — a specific kind of ear-pendant — and it has a life of its own in the south. At the Jambukeśvara temple at Tiruvanaikkaval the goddess is said to wear tāṭaṅkas in the form of Śrīcakras, installed, tradition holds, by Śaṅkara himself to temper her fierceness; the story is widely told and impossible to date, but it shows how heavily this particular ornament is freighted.

Making the sun and moon her earrings puts her body on a cosmic scale for the first time since the third verse drowned the world-eggs in her light. The two luminaries hang at the level of the face, one on each side, and the reader is expected to hold the small image and the enormous one at once without choosing between them. This is the ordinary logic of the aṅga-varṇana in a hymn to a supreme deity: the description must stay a description of a woman's face and must also be a description of everything.

There is a small philological prize buried in the second name. The word printed here as oḍupa does not exist independently. The dictionary knows uḍupa — a raft, and, because the half-moon is shaped like a boat, the moon. Tapana, the sun, plus uḍupa gives tapanoḍupa, because a final a and an initial u merge into o. The o at the seam is the sandhi, not the word. Anyone hunting oḍupa in Monier-Williams will find nothing; the moon in her ear is a little boat.
commentary.practice:
This verse contains what is probably the rarest character you will meet in the whole thousand names. Kḷpta is written कॢप्त, with the vowel sign ॢ — the syllabic ḷ, which has its own place in the alphabet between ṝ and e, its own independent letter ऌ, and almost no words to appear in. In the entire Lalitā Sahasranāma it occurs exactly twice: here at name twenty-one, and again at name one hundred and twenty-eight in līlākḷpta. Both are forms of the root kḷp, to arrange or fashion, which is very nearly the only root that uses it. Pronounce it as a syllabic l — the l itself carrying the beat, as in the second syllable of "little" said quickly — although most reciters in practice say something close to klipta, and that is the accepted convention. Either way, it is worth stopping to look at the character, because you are unlikely to see it again.

The two ornament words are consonant exercises of different kinds. Kadambamañjarī has the conjunct ñj, in which the palatal nasal is made at exactly the place of the j that follows it. Tāṭaṅka runs a retroflex ṭ, then a second retroflex ṭ, then the guttural nasal of ṅk — three places of articulation in five syllables, with the tongue travelling back, staying back, and then dropping to the velum.

Yugalībhūta contains a piece of grammar worth naming. Yugala, a pair, becomes yugalī- before a form of the root bhū: the final vowel lengthens to ī and the whole thing means "having become a pair". Sanskrit grammarians call this the cvi construction, and it turns any noun into a verb of becoming. Her sun and moon have not been made into earrings; they have become a pair of earrings. Hearing the ī as a grammatical marker rather than as part of the stem makes the compound fall apart cleanly.

The two lines are metrically very different in feel. The first is light and quick — kadamba, mañjarī and manohara are all built of short syllables and open vowels — while the second is heavy from tāṭaṅka onwards, with the long ā of tāṭaṅka and yugalībhūta weighing it down. Let that difference stand rather than evening the line out. The flower is light and the sun and the moon are not.

For contemplation: the verse offers a good exercise in holding two magnitudes at once. Look at the sprig of blossom. Then look at the earrings. Then try to keep both in the same picture without letting either become a symbol of the other.

009.subtitle: Ruby mirrors and coral put to shame

commentary.meaning: Cheeks and lips, and both names are built as contests that the thing compared loses. The first says that the expanse of her cheek defeats a mirror cut from ruby — which is a claim about colour, about polish, and about the reflection you would see in either. The second says her lips shame the beauty of fresh coral and of the bimba fruit, the two things a Sanskrit poet is expected to reach for when describing a red mouth. Both names produce a standard of comparison and then knock it over. The figure has a name in Sanskrit poetics, vyatireka, where the thing described surpasses the thing it is described by, and having two of them back to back gives this verse an argumentative edge that the purely descriptive verses before it do not have.
commentary.history:
Padmarāga is the third distinct word for a ruby in the first ten verses of this text. The meditation verse crowned her with māṇikya; the fourth verse strung her diadem with kuruvinda; now her cheeks are compared to a slab of padmarāga, literally "lotus-coloured". Three words, one stone, and the same red that has run through every verse since the first. A mirror of ruby is, incidentally, a fantasy object — mirrors in classical India were polished metal — which sharpens the boast. The poet has invented the most extravagant reflecting surface he can and then said her cheek is better.

The lips are compared to two things and both are conventional to the point of exhaustion. Vidruma is coral, imported and costly, the standard red of jewellery. Bimba is the ripe fruit of Coccinia grandis, the ivy gourd, a small scarlet ovoid, and comparing a woman's lower lip to it is so entrenched in Sanskrit that bimbādhara, "bimba-lipped", is simply a word for beautiful. When this name says her lips put the bimba to shame, the target is partly the cliché. Śaṅkara does the same thing at greater length, proposing coral as a comparison and then dismissing the bimba as too embarrassed even to get onto the scales.

One genuinely useful thing about this verse is that it preserves a variant. The source this site is built from records, beside radanacchadā, the alternative reading daśanacchadā. Radana and daśana are two different words for a tooth, and either compounded with chada, a cover, gives "that which covers the teeth" — a lip. The sense is identical and the manuscripts disagree about which word was used. It is worth knowing that this happens, and that the tradition has kept the alternatives in the margin rather than silently choosing. A thousand-name hymn transmitted for centuries by memory and by copyists will have such places, and pretending otherwise would misrepresent the text.

Finally, a grammatical oddity that is easy to miss while chanting. Almost every one of the thousand names is a feminine nominative singular ending in long ā. This one does not: kapolabhūḥ ends in a visarga, because kapola-bhū is a feminine noun in ū meaning the ground or region of the cheek. In the first sixty names only two behave this way — this one and mahālāvaṇyaśevadhiḥ at forty-eight. When the ending changes in a text this regular, it is a small event.
commentary.practice:
Start with the visarga, because this is the first name in the stotra that ends in one. A visarga is a voiceless breath that takes its colour from the vowel before it, so kapolabhūḥ ends with a faint echoing hu — bhū-hu, very light, released rather than pronounced. Reciters differ in how much of it they give at a pause; almost all give something. Establishing the habit here will serve for the rest of the hymn.

Two compounds in this verse end in -in stems that have lost their n. Paribhāvin, "defying, putting down", appears as paribhāvi-; nyakkārin, "humiliating", appears as nyakkāri-. This is what always happens to an -in stem inside a compound, and once you have seen it twice in one verse you will recognise it everywhere.

The hardest single word is nyakkāri. It opens with ny — the palatal nasal followed by y, both made at the hard palate — and then doubles the k. Say it as nyak-kā-ri and give the doubled consonant its full length; the metre depends on it.

Radanacchadā hides a sandhi rule worth learning because it is so common. The second element is chada, a cover. After a short vowel, an initial ch is doubled to cch, so radana plus chada gives radanacchada, written रदनच्छदा with c and ch joined. Anywhere in Sanskrit that a word beginning in ch follows a short vowel, expect this.

For the rest of the consonants: padmarāga opens with the cluster dm, dental into labial; śilādarśa has ś at the start and the sequence rś in ādarśa, so the palatal sibilant appears twice with a retroflex-adjacent r between them; and vidruma has dr. The second line is also, incidentally, the first place in the stotra where two words for the same colour sit in the same compound — vidruma and bimba are both simply "red", and hearing them as a pair rather than as two separate comparisons is what makes the line land.

On what to hold while chanting: this is a good verse to notice that the hymn is not naive. It knows the comparisons are worn out, it uses them anyway, and it defeats them on purpose. There is a kind of devotion in that which is quite different from awe.

010.subtitle: Teeth like sprouts of pure knowledge

commentary.meaning: The mouth, in two names that could hardly be further apart in register. The first says her two rows of teeth shine like the sprouts of Śuddhavidyā — and the comparison stops the reader, because Śuddhavidyā is not a plant. It is the pure knowledge, in this tradition the name of the mantra itself, so the image is of a mantra sown like a seed and coming up in rows behind her lips. The second name leaves the body: the fragrance of the camphor-scented betel roll in her mouth reaches out and draws in the quarters of space. Nothing is described in that second name except a smell and a direction of travel. The mouth that has just been given rows of sprouting mantra is the mouth whose breath pulls the horizons toward it, and since this hymn is itself something spoken out of that mouth's tradition, it is a good place for the first ten verses to end.
commentary.history:
Śuddhavidyā, pure knowledge, is a technical term. In the Śaiva systems it names one of the tattvas, a level of reality; in Śrīvidyā it is above all a name for the fifteen-syllabled mantra of this tradition, the vidyā itself. Comparing teeth to its sprouts is therefore not a simile drawn from the garden but a doctrinal statement in the shape of one. The mantra is planted, and what comes up out of the soil, visible when she smiles, is a row of white shoots. It is also a claim about origins: the sound that the mantra is made of is formed at the teeth as much as anywhere.

The word for tooth here is dvija, and the dictionary gives it three meanings that are all live in Sanskrit: a tooth, because it grows twice; a bird, because it is born first as an egg; and a man of the first three classes, twice-born through initiation. The rows in her mouth are therefore rows of the twice-born, and the pun is not accidental in a text that will shortly be describing her assembly of attendants. Sanskrit lets a poet say something like this without doing anything but choosing the ordinary word.

The betel roll of the second name is a specific ritual object. A vīṭikā is betel leaf wrapped around areca nut and lime with spices, here perfumed with camphor, and offering tāmbūla is one of the standard services in formal worship, given after food. It is offered to this goddess in Śrīvidyā practice, and the hymn returns to it: at name five hundred and fifty-nine she is tāmbūlapūritamukhī, her mouth full of betel. The opening invocation printed before this stotra uses the same phrase. So the detail travels — from the devotee's tray, into the goddess's mouth, and back out as a fragrance that fills the directions.

Camphor is worth a moment. Monier-Williams records that both mṛgāṅka and śaśāṅka — deer-marked and hare-marked, the two everyday Sanskrit names for the moon — are also names for camphor, because of its whiteness and its coolness. The moon that was on her forehead in the fifth verse and hanging from her ear in the eighth is therefore in her mouth here, in a different state of matter. Whether the Vāgdevatās intended that is unknowable; that the vocabulary makes it available is a fact about the language they were writing in.

One word does more than it appears to. Samākarṣin means drawing together, attracting — and Monier-Williams, unusually, gives "diffusing fragrance" as one of its senses outright, so the compound is idiomatic rather than strained. The scent does not spread. It pulls. Digantara, the last element, means a quarter of the sky, another region, and simply space. The final image of these ten verses is of the horizons being drawn inward toward a mouth.
commentary.practice:
The line divides into two sixteen-syllable names as usual, and both of them end with a sandhi that has swallowed a vowel. Dvaya plus ujjvalā gives dvayojjvalā, a and u merging into o; that same ujjvalā appeared at the end of the second verse, so the ear should recognise it. Vidyā plus aṅkura gives vidyāṅkura, and aṅkura plus ākāra gives aṅkurākāra: two separate mergers into a long ā, both invisible, one after the other. If the first name feels like an undifferentiated wall of syllables, it is because three word-boundaries in it have been erased. Rebuild it as śuddha - vidyā - aṅkura - ākāra - dvija - paṅkti - dvaya - ujjvalā and it becomes a sentence.

The doubled j of ujjvalā followed by v is the hardest cluster in the verse and the same one that ended the second verse; take it as -yoj-jva-lā. Paṅkti puts a guttural nasal, a k and a t together with one vowel among them: paṅk-ti. And dvija and dvaya both begin with dv, a dental followed by the labiodental v, which English speakers tend to reduce to a d or a plain v — both consonants must be heard.

In the second name, karpūra has the sequence rp with a long ū after it, vīṭikā has a retroflex ṭ between two long vowels, and samākarṣi has the retroflex ṣ. Keep the ṣ of -karṣi distinct from the s of sam- at the start of the same word: one word, two sibilants, two places of articulation.

One more instance of an ending you have now met several times: samākarṣin has lost its n inside the compound, exactly as paribhāvin and nyakkārin did in the previous verse.

This verse is also a natural place to stop and take stock of the breath. The head-to-foot description will continue for another twenty-five names — speech, smile, chin, throat — but the ten verses covered here form a unit: the manifestation, the weapons, the flood of light, and then the face from the hair down to the mouth. Reciting the ten together takes only a few minutes, and doing so is a good way to feel the shape of the opening before going further.

For contemplation, the last name gives an unusually simple instruction. Attend to a fragrance, and notice that it is described as pulling rather than spreading. Then notice that the thousand names you are reciting came out of the same mouth.

crossReferences.translation: Mother — Skanda, Indra and Viṣṇu, having beaten the demons in battle, come back with their helmets off and their armour still on, and turn away from the leavings of Śiva's own offering, which are Caṇḍa's share; and the mouthfuls of betel from your mouth, bright with flakes of camphor pale as the moon, dissolve on their tongues.
crossReferences.relevance: The same camphor and the same betel, and an unexpectedly domestic scene built around them: the great gods come back from a war and go straight for what is in her mouth rather than for the formal offering. It is worth reading beside a name that says her betel's fragrance draws in the horizons, because it shows what the tradition thinks that pull is actually like.

crossReferences.translation: The cakora birds drank the net of moonlight that is your smile, from that moon which is your face, and it was so rich that their beaks went numb. So now, wanting something sour, they drink up the nectar-waves of the ordinary cold-rayed moon, night after night, as freely as if it were sour gruel.
crossReferences.relevance: The teeth of this verse only appear when she smiles, and this is what the tradition makes of that smile: light so concentrated that the birds who live on moonlight are ruined for the real moon. It also completes the sequence of moons that has run through these ten verses — the half-moon on her brow, the moon in her ear, the moonlight of her smile, and camphor, which shares its name with the moon.

crossReferences.translation: Her red outdoing the flush of the hibiscus flower; bearing the noose and the goad, and the bow and arrows too; her eyes copper-coloured, her ornament a garland of red flowers, her mouth full of betel — to Tripurā I bow.
crossReferences.relevance: The verse that opens the whole manuscript, twenty pages before this one. It has the same four weapons as the stotra's second and third verses, the same red, and the same mouth full of betel that this verse describes; and the phrase tāmbūlapūritamukhī will come back as a name in its own right at number five hundred and fifty-nine. The detail is old and settled, and the hymn is working inside an image that was already fixed.
